subsection: 4. Pathways to excellence in physical activity

notes.h: What a pathway to excellence is
notes.b: Nobody becomes a high-level performer overnight. A pathway to excellence is the route, and the supports along it, that take a participant from first involvement in a sport to high-level performance.
points: A typical route runs from school or club to county or regional development squads (teams that select and train promising players), then to provincial and national underage squads, and on to senior international level.
Athletes move up the pathway as their skill and commitment develop, and each stage needs suitable coaching, competition and facilities, so a gap at any stage can hold a talented athlete back.
notes.tip: When asked to describe a pathway, give the stages in order from school or club up to senior international level, and mention the supports (coaching, competition, facilities) that each stage needs.

notes.b: Long-term athlete development is a model associated with Istvan Balyi. It matches training and competition to the age and stage of the athlete, because what suits a seven-year-old is wrong for an elite adult.
points: FUNdamentals: children build fundamental movement skills such as running, jumping, throwing and catching through play, with enjoyment at the centre, so they want to keep taking part.
Learn to Train: children learn the basic skills of sport in a structured way, still across a range of activities rather than one sport.
Train to Train: the training load (how much and how hard an athlete trains) increases, building the fitness and skill base for later competition.
Train to Compete: training is targeted at the demands of competition in the chosen sport and position.
Train to Win: performance at the highest level, with specialised, individual training aimed at peaking (being at their very best) for major events.
Active for Life: everyone, at any level, is encouraged to stay active throughout life, as a participant, coach, official or volunteer.
Early specialisation, focusing on one sport at too young an age, can cause drop-out and injury, which is why the early stages stay broad and playful.
notes.tip: Learn the six stage names in order: FUNdamentals, Learn to Train, Train to Train, Train to Compete, Train to Win, Active for Life. Remember that Active for Life is for everyone, not only elite athletes.

notes.h: Strengthening pathways between school and community sport
notes.b: Many pupils enjoy PE at school but never join a local club, and the pathway breaks at that point. These are ways school-based and community-based (club) activity can be linked more closely.
points: Club coaches run sessions in schools, and teachers coach in clubs, so pupils meet club coaches in a familiar setting and each side learns from the other.
Taster sessions and bring-a-friend days move pupils from school PE into local clubs, because trying a club with a friend is less daunting than joining alone.
Shared facilities and coordinated fixtures (matches scheduled to avoid clashes) stop school and club demands from clashing.
Information on local clubs is given to pupils, and clubs hold open days, so pupils know what is available and how to join.
Transition Year sports-leadership and coaching courses train young pupils to lead and coach, giving them skills and a route into club involvement.
Local Sports Partnerships link schools and clubs, and school-based clubs are affiliated to national governing bodies (NGBs, the organisations that run each sport nationally).
School and club coaches communicate about workload, to avoid overtraining talented young players who may be training and playing for both.
notes.tip: If asked for two ways to strengthen the pathway, choose two distinct ideas, such as club coaches in schools and taster sessions, and say how each moves pupils from school into a club.

notes.b: Once a player shows talent, a series of structures gives them better coaching and tougher competition at each step of the pathway.
points: Clubs are the first structure, providing regular coaching and competition.
County or regional development squads select and develop talented players.
Provincial and national underage squads give young athletes higher-level competition.
Academies, such as the rugby provincial academies, give selected players structured, intensive development.
College sports scholarships support athletes who combine study with training, so they do not have to choose between education and sport.

notes.b: High performance is expensive, because it needs coaches, facilities, travel and support staff. Money reaches athletes through several routes.
points: Sport Ireland funds national governing bodies for high performance, so each NGB can pay for coaching and squad programmes.
Direct funding goes to high-performing athletes through Sport Ireland's International Carding Scheme.
University sports scholarships support students who compete at a high level.
Sponsorship from companies adds income for athletes and teams.
notes.tip: For how an NGB might use funding to support high performance, link the money to something specific such as coaching, facilities or camps. Do not quote funding amounts or carding levels.

notes.b: Talent needs expert support and the right places to train. Elite athletes rely on specialist people as well as good facilities.
points: Qualified high-performance coaches work with squads and individual athletes, planning training to a high standard.
Strength and conditioning, physiotherapy, performance analysis, nutrition and psychology support athletes, covering their fitness, injuries, technique, diet and mental preparation.
Many of these services are delivered through the Sport Ireland Institute, which provides high-performance support services to athletes and national governing bodies.
The Sport Ireland Campus at Abbotstown, Dublin, is a national centre for high performance, bringing facilities and expertise together in one place.
County grounds and indoor arenas provide local training space, so athletes can train close to home.

notes.b: Athletes improve by being tested, so the pathway has to supply regular competition at the right level.
points: Regular high-level competition at underage and senior level tests athletes against strong opponents, which pushes their skills and fitness on.
International fixtures and training camps prepare athletes for competition abroad, where conditions and opposition are unfamiliar.

notes.h: Worked analysis: a Gaelic game (Gaelic football)
notes.b: Gaelic football is governed by the GAA, and its players are amateurs who train around work or study, not paid professionals. Analysing it means judging strengths and weaknesses of the supports and suggesting improvements.
points: Pathway: the club system gives young players a local route from school into club teams and then into county squads.
Strength: the voluntary club system is deep and widespread across local communities, so almost every young player has a club nearby.
Strength: clubs and schools are closely linked, so pupils can move from school games into club teams.
Competition: club and county championships give players competitive experience.
Weakness: most support relies on volunteers, which limits the time and expertise available for high performance.
Weakness: amateur players train around work or study, which limits the training time they can give to high performance.
Improvement: more funded development officers and coach education would strengthen the link between club coaches and high-performance squads.
notes.tip: Describe Gaelic players as amateurs, never as paid professionals. A good analysis names the activity, gives strengths and weaknesses of the provision, and ends with a suggested improvement.

notes.b: Swimming is an Olympic sport, governed in Ireland by Swim Ireland. It shows how a sport with national facilities and carded athletes is supported.
points: Pathway: swimming clubs and school-based clubs feed talented swimmers into development squads and then national squads.
Funding: Sport Ireland funds Swim Ireland for high performance, and high-performing swimmers can receive direct funding through the International Carding Scheme.
Facilities: the National Aquatic Centre, on the Sport Ireland Campus at Abbotstown, Dublin, gives elite swimmers a national high-performance base.
Competition: international fixtures and training camps give swimmers experience against strong opponents abroad.
Strength: concentrating a national centre and its expertise in one place gives elite swimmers a focused environment.
Weakness: reliance on a small number of national facilities concentrates access in one place.
Weakness: direct funding goes to carded athletes, so swimmers outside the scheme receive less direct support.
Improvement: spreading access to high-performance facilities beyond one national centre, and extending support to swimmers outside the carding scheme.
notes.tip: For how an NGB supports high performance in swimming, use funding from Sport Ireland, the pathway of squads, and the national facility. Keep to the facts and do not invent amounts.

keyTerms.definition: The route and supports by which a participant progresses from first involvement to high-level performance.
A model that matches training and competition to the age and stage of the athlete, with active for life as its aim for everyone.
Focusing on one sport at a young age, which can cause drop-out and injury.
A squad that selects and trains promising players so they can move up a pathway.
A squad for players below senior age, selected to compete at provincial or national level.
A structured programme that gives selected players intensive development and coaching.
Support for athletes who combine study with training and competition.
A Sport Ireland scheme that gives direct funding to high-performing athletes.
A body that provides high-performance support services to athletes and national governing bodies.
A short introductory session that lets pupils try an activity before joining a club.
Scientific support, such as strength and conditioning, nutrition, physiotherapy and psychology, used to improve performance.

questions.prompt: Analyse the provision and support for excellence in performance in a named physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Swimming is governed by Swim Ireland. Pathway: swimming clubs and school-based clubs feed talented swimmers into development squads and then national squads. Provision: the National Aquatic Centre on the Sport Ireland Campus at Abbotstown, Dublin, gives elite swimmers a national high-performance base, supported by Sport Ireland funding to Swim Ireland. Coaching and science: qualified high-performance coaches and performance support are available, many of them delivered through the Sport Ireland Institute. Competition: swimmers take part in international fixtures and attend training camps abroad. Strength: a national centre concentrates expertise and facilities in one place. Weakness: direct funding for individual athletes goes through the International Carding Scheme, so swimmers outside the scheme have less direct support, and reliance on a small number of national facilities limits access.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways in which pathways between school sport and community sport can be strengthened.
questions.model: 1. Club coaches run sessions in schools and teachers coach in clubs, so pupils meet trained coaches in both settings and the move from school to club is easier. 2. Taster sessions and bring-a-friend days introduce pupils to local clubs, so they can join a club with friends and with confidence.
